I have said this to every new person we hire since. The licence covered the hardback and nothing else, and it said so in one line, and everybody in this building assumed that a cover licence covered the book, in every form the book would ever take. That assumption is not written down anywhere. It is just there, the way water is there. The paperback was approved on a Tuesday morning and nine people saw that file, and not one of them opened the licence, because by then the cover had stopped being a decision and had become a fact. You do not check a fact. What would I do differently? One thing, and it is boring. I would put the limits of every licence on the front page of the file, in a single line, in a place you cannot scroll past. Not in the contract. On the file. And I will tell you what I would not do, because it was the first thing three people suggested. Blaming the designer would have been easy, and it would have changed nothing, because she was never the person who signed it. If I had let that happen, I would have lost the only person in the room who actually knew what had gone on that morning.

There is one question I ask in every session, and I ask it in the same place: after both opening statements, and before anybody says a number. What would you have done differently? Not what went wrong, and not whose fault it was. What would you have done differently. It sounds soft and it is the hardest working question I have. Here is why it works. It is the only question in the room that nobody can lose. Saying what you would have done differently is not the same as saying you were wrong, and everybody in that room knows the difference, so they answer it honestly, often for the first time in two years. And once one side has said it out loud, the other side stops defending, because there is nothing left to defend against. What happens when somebody refuses? It happens, and I let it. I just note it, and I can tell you that side almost always ends up paying more. A room that has heard no regret has nothing to build a compromise out of. You cannot construct an agreement out of two people who are both still completely right.
